analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal excise taxes on luxury cars, boats, aircraft, jewelry, and furs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 110 sponsors but never got a House vote; Congress instead phased out most of the luxury taxes that year through a broader budget bill.
analysis.plain_summary: The luxury excise taxes, created in 1990, charged extra tax on expensive passenger cars, boats, airplanes, jewelry, and furs, with the stated goal of raising money from high-end buyers. This bill would have repealed all of them on the day it was signed. It went to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote. Months later, the House pointed the bill to H.R. 2264, the 1993 budget law, which Congress passed later that year with a partial repeal of the same taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Buyers of high-end cars, boats, aircraft, jewelry, and furs — mostly higher-income households — would pay less at purchase. The industries that build and sell those goods would sell more if the tax was depressing sales.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Buyers of yachts, jets, furs, jewelry

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals subchapter A of chapter 31 of the Internal Revenue Code, the section imposing the luxury excise taxes on passenger vehicles, boats, aircraft, jewelry, and furs, effective on enactment.
The CRS summary confirms the bill repeals the luxury excise tax on passenger vehicles, boats, aircraft, jewelry, and furs.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally, would lose the revenue those taxes raised, shifting a bit of the federal tax burden away from buyers of luxury goods and onto everyone else.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the taxes gives up federal revenue; the luxury taxes were enacted in 1990 specifically to raise money from buyers of expensive goods, so repeal moves that burden to other taxpayers.
The repeal takes effect immediately on enactment, with no phaseout, so the revenue loss would hit right away.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward tax cut for high-end purchases and the industries that make them. Supporters argued the taxes hurt manufacturing jobs in boat and aircraft building; the cost is forgone federal revenue and a tax code that asks slightly less of the wealthiest purchasers. The bill itself was badly designed in one respect: an immediate full repeal maximizes the revenue hole. In the end Congress chose a middle path — phasing out most of the taxes rather than repealing them all at once.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote; in August the House pointed the matter to the 1993 budget reconciliation bill, and the luxury taxes were substantially phased out through that law instead.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 22, 1993, with 109 cosponsors joining sponsor Jim Saxton, and was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
The committee took no further action — no markup and no vote were ever scheduled; the next entry in the action history, on August 10, 1993, reads only 'See H.R. 2264.'

H.R. 2264, the 1993 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act, was the major budget bill of that Congress, and it repealed the luxury tax on boats and phased out the taxes on jewelry, furs, and aircraft while reducing the car tax — accomplishing much of this bill's goal through the budget process instead.
The bill itself was never reported out of committee and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Buyers of luxury goods and the boat, jewelry, fur, aircraft, and auto industries came out ahead: they got most of the repeal they wanted, delivered through the 1993 budget law, while the bill's sponsors got their goal without the Treasury losing the full revenue at once.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Luxury goods buyers and their industries

for.name: Rep. Jim Saxton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the luxury excise taxes.

for.name: 109 House members
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 97 Republicans and 12 Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill; it received no markup and no vote, and the House instead directed the matter to the budget reconciliation bill.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list was 97 Republicans and 12 Democrats, so the bill had clear Republican support with a modest bipartisan fringe, but no floor vote ever revealed how the chamber as a whole would have split.

industries.note: The tax on boats over $100,000 had been blamed for collapsing sales and boatyard job losses, and it was the first luxury tax Congress repealed in the 1993 budget law. Repeal helps the industry and its buyers, with the cost being forgone federal revenue from high-end purchases.
The bill removes the excise tax on aircraft, and the 1993 budget law later phased it out. Lower prices for private planes benefit wealthy buyers, funded by other taxpayers.
Repeal eliminates the tax on jewelry purchases over $10,000, a direct boost to high-end jewelry sales.
The luxury tax on furs was repealed, lifting a levy the industry saw as damaging sales.
The bill repeals the tax on expensive passenger cars outright; the eventual budget law chose a phase-down instead, so this bill is more generous to the industry than what passed.
The luxury taxes were designed to fall on buyers of expensive goods; repeal shifts that revenue burden to taxpayers as a whole.
